props.title: High Anxiety
props.initialSlug: A Hitchcock spoof from the mind of Mel Brooks

sections.content: Mel Brooks's loving tribute to Alfred Hitchcock's thriller canon, High Anxiety (1977) stands as both parody and homage, directly referencing classics like Vertigo (1958), The Birds (1963), and Psycho (1960). Brooks himself stars as Dr. Richard Thorndyke, a psychiatrist with a fear of heights who becomes entangled in murder and conspiracy. The film's genius lies in how it maintains narrative tension while delivering pitch-perfect comedy, particularly in scenes like the newspaper attack (spoofing The Birds) and the shower scene featuring the deadly newspaper (mocking Psycho's infamous murder).

sections.content: The film represents a crucial moment in comedy-thriller hybrids, paving the way for later genre parodies like Airplane! (1980) and Hot Shots! (1991). Brooks's attention to technical detail - including recreating Hitchcock's signature camera movements and Bernard Herrmann-style musical cues - elevates High Anxiety beyond mere spoof into skilled cinematic homage. The film's influence can be seen in later works like Scary Movie (1999) and A Haunted House (2013), though few achieve Brooks's balance of reverence and ridicule.

Worth noting is Brooks's masterful understanding of Hitchcock's visual language. The film's opening shot, tracking through the airport, mirrors North by Northwest (1959), while the tower sequences deliberately echo Vertigo. Brooks even includes Hitchcock's signature cameo tradition, appearing himself multiple times in a self-referential twist on the master's technique. SUBHEAD: The Art of Cinematic Parody

sections.content: High Anxiety exemplifies the sophisticated parody style that defined Brooks's best work, including Young Frankenstein (1974) and Blazing Saddles (1974). Unlike later spoof films that relied primarily on reference humor, Brooks crafted genuine characters and coherent plots while layering in his satirical elements. The film's success influenced decades of genre parody, though few achieved its delicate balance of homage and humor.
